Resolution #3 Title & Author “Towards a Clear Multifaceted Strategy for Labor” by Annabel V., Sacramento DSA; Benjamin D. & Ryan M., Metro DC DSA; and Emmanuel S., New Orleans DSA. Budget Analysis Staff Costs $74,610 National priority - full time staffer. NOTE: currently national priorities committees have nowhere near a full time staffer. They have part of the time of a field organizer. But this resolution calls for a full time staffer to be hired. 12% Overhead $8,953 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $0 Resolve Therefore be it resolved, that the Democratic Socialist Labor Commission (DSLC) shall focus its activity on supporting the development of chapter-level labor formations made up of workers regardless of the unionization status of their workplace; and shall restructure itself to be comprised of members of recognized chapter-level labor formations; and be it Resolved, the National Political Committee (NPC) shall hire at least one (1) staff labor organizer dedicated solely to supporting the DSLC and local chapter-level labor formations; and be it Resolved, that the DSLC shall develop programming for regional workplace organizing schools alongside partnering with our youth section to revive DSA’s Campus Labor Institutes; and that these educational initiatives shall be conceived along the following lines: 1) to educate DSA members and the general public about the labor movement, 2) to hold workplace organizer trainings for workers in organized and unorganized workplaces and industries, 3) to proactively include workers from traditionally marginalized backgrounds and job classifications, and 4) to subsidize, to the extent possible, the costs of access and participation for low- wage workers; and be it Resolved, that the overall strategy of the DSLC shall be informed by strategic assessments of local conditions, and shall therefore be focused on developing local DSA labor networks that can pursue the following goals: 1) organizing within unions where they exist, especially when doing so provides opportunities to leverage demands against the state for the common good of the working class in general, 2) organizing within strategic industries, particularly where the potential economic impact on capital is greatest, and 3) leading efforts to organize workers in key unorganized sectors.

[PDF page 13] Background Information Whereas, the inertia of neoliberal economics presses workers deeper into poverty and insecurity, while it simultaneously demands the disempowerment, demobilization, and disenfranchisement of workers as a political class; and Whereas, over the last sixty years, the organizations that workers forged through struggle as vehicles for their demands have been systematically attacked through deliberate campaigns of legislative and judicial obstruction, public intimidation, and often violence; and Whereas, labor is not a finite single-issue campaign but an ongoing foundational component of our political project, one which does not merely seek to improve the economic conditions of workers, but does so in pursuit of working-class political power and in the name of working-class agency; and Whereas, across the US, right-to-work laws and decades of deindustrialization have gutted traditional labor strongholds, as millions of workers have flooded into growing sectors such as service and logistics, and as historic and current racial and gender disparities across sectors have left many workers without representation; and Whereas, our aim must not only be to defend and strengthen the already-existing labor movement but to capture new territory by leading efforts to organize workers in key unorganized sectors; and Whereas, our goal should be to build an organization with the credibility and strength to one day call hundreds of thousands of workers out to strike when necessary, the path to building such an organization will require a clear strategy, with flexibility based on the diversity of regional labor conditions, along with a serious commitment from our members and their national bodies.

Resolution #4 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Building the DSA International Committee” by Jack S. L. of Los Angeles DSA; Morgan D., Alec D., and Emmanuel S. of New Orleans DSA Staff Costs $861 Few hours per month, same as existing support to national working groups (internal and external communications, website updates, Zoom calls, organizing coaching.) 12% Overhead $103 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $964 Resolve Therefore be it resolved, that the Convention directs the National Political Committee (NPC) to cooperate with the International Committee to meet the following goals: 1) to establish relations with left, socialist, and working class organizations across the world through a strategic vetting process accountable to the NPC, 2) to offer material and symbolic forms of solidarity to left movements, organizations, communities, and individuals targeted by hostile institutions and social forces in other countries, 3) to support the political and economic struggles of migrant workers and immigrants in the U.S., 4) to educate, advise, and organize the general membership on international matters, and 5) to foster coordination between the International Committee, and local Chapters and Regional Organizations; and be it Resolved, that the International Committee shall prioritize establishing relations with socialist and working class organizations in Mexico, Puerto Rico, Canada, Brazil, the Caribbean, and Latin America broadly, especially organizations with a genuinely mass character; and be it Resolved, that the NPC through the International Committee shall be required to issue to the general membership of DSA quarterly bulletins disseminating news and analysis of major international developments, as well as annual reports documenting Committee activity, progress, and expectations due by the first day of every year; and be it Resolved, that the NPC through the International Committee shall develop clear rules and standards governing membership in the Committee, and shall make these rules known to the general membership of DSA; and that all Committee membership rules and standards shall be bound by the following conditions: 1) that only DSA members in-good-standing shall be eligible for Committee membership, 2) that Committee members shall reflect the democratic socialist and internationalist values of the organization as a whole; and 3) that the Committee shall privilege applicants who are undocumented workers, migrant workers, immigrants, or the children thereof.

[PDF page 15] Background Information Whereas, all countries exist economically within the system of the global market, and politically within systems of imperialism which will only be effectively dismantled and replaced through the international collaboration and organization of the working classes of all countries and nationalities; and Whereas, the US working class is itself multinational, internationalism at home means developing concrete steps to support and integrate the struggles of immigrant and migrant workers in the US—these include struggles for political rights as well as economic struggles embedded within the broader labor movement; and Whereas, an effective and orderly International Committee is necessary for DSA to transition into an internationalist organization, one through which immigrants and workers of color can build power and address needs.

Staff Costs $74,610 National priority - full time staffer 12% Overhead $8,953 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $83,563 Resolve Be it therefore resolved, the Democratic Socialists of America will make defense of immigrant and refugee rights a top national priority of the organization; and Be it further resolved, the Democratic Socialists of America reaffirms our position that no human being is illegal and that all working and oppressed people are welcome in our organization on an equal basis regardless of immigration or citizenship status; and Be it further resolved, the Democratic Socialists of America support the struggle of immigrant communities, including around partial demands (such as restoring DACA) as well as the right of immigrants and their communities to lead this struggle and determine its tactics; and Be it further resolved, the Democratic Socialists of America demand: • Abolition of ICE and an end to the persecution, jailing and deportation of immigrants. • Permanent resident status, including a path to citizenship, for all immigrants living in the United States. • Aid to those fleeing from violence, political and economic turmoil as well as global warming induced climate catastrophes instead of jailing refugees. • Full labor rights and integration in the labor movement for immigrant workers. • Repeal of employer sanctions and no expansion of guest worker programs. • An end to the Muslim Ban and discrimination in the issuance of visas. • A firm and unequivocal stance in favor of immigrants, refugees and their communities from all candidates claiming to oppose Trumpism. Resolution #6 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Orienting to Latinx Communities” by José G. P. of Metro Atlanta DSA. Staff Costs $9,326 Project management and overseeing major website edits. 12% Overhead $1,119 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $10,445 Author’s Estimated Cost Could vary greatly depending on how the NPC chooses to implement the resolution. Minimally, $10 for a domain name and +/- 50 hours of staff time for coordination a year, assuming that we use the same hosting as the national web site and have volunteers doing the editorial work. Resolve Background Information Be it resolved, the National Political Committee will establish a Spanish-language DSA web site with a goal of launching within 90 days after the 2019 DSA convention, if possible. The web site should have both translations and material directly generated for it. Be it further resolved, the National Political Committee will initiate the selection of an editorial board for the web site to include a diverse group of Latinx and other comrades, especially those fluent in Spanish, but without precluding the inclusion of others. Be it further resolved, in collaboration with the National Political Committee, this editorial board shall have the additional responsibilities of developing our work with Latinx communities, establishing relations with organizations, and promoting collaboration and the exchange of information between Locals involved in this work. Be it finally resolved, these additional responsibilities are not meant to be permanent but a transitional step towards the creation by the NPC of a working group or other body focused on the Latinx communities and their issues. Whereas: The Latinx communities are now the largest oppressed minority in the country, with 18% of the country’s population, some 60 million people, and concentrated among young people. One in five millennials is classified as “Hispanic” by the census bureau; among post-millennials, one in four. Whereas: The United States has the second largest number of Spanish-speaking people in the world after Mexico, some 55 million people over the age of five. Some 41 million over that age are considered native speakers as that is the main language used in their homes, a number comparable to native speakers in Colombia, Argentina and Spain itself.

[PDF page 19] Whereas: Due to common oppression, language and cultural elements, as well as modern communications and mass media, these communities have developed a common political identity as shown, for example, by the millions who marched for immigrant rights in the spring of 2006. Whereas: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a millennial Puerto Rican woman and democratic socialist, has become by far the single most prominent Latinx political figure in the community and media, presenting extraordinary opportunities for the DSA. Whereas: Addressing the Latinx community in the Spanish language is both a needed practical measure and an important political statement given the size of the DSA and its national presence. Whereas: A socialist transformation of the United States is unthinkable without the massive, militant participation of Latinx working people.

Resolution #7 Title & Author “A Conflict Resolution Training Program for DSA” by Christian E. of Mid-Missouri DSA; Jeffrey A. of Seattle DSA; Kim L. of Metro DC DSA; Roe C. of Cincinnati/North Kentucky DSA; Sauce of North Bay DSA OC; Yesenia P. of San Diego DSA. Budget Analysis Staff Costs $18,652 Staff time to coordinate - estimated 1/4 time staffer. 12% Overhead $2,238 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $20,891 Author’s Estimated Costs Resolve The following costs will need to be covered by DSA: (1) cost of external training and materials for the CRCWG, (2) cost of external consultant(s) and advisor(s) if needed, (3) cost of CRCWG meetings and collaboration tools (e.g. Zoom) (4) cost of printing/publishing materials, and (5) cost of trainings, including travel. Be it therefore resolved, DSA shall create an internal Conflict Resolution Curriculum Working Group (CRCWG), and the CRCWG shall develop an internal Conflict Resolution training program; and Be it further resolved, the CRCWG shall: (1) be a minimum of 6 members, (2) shall consist of self-selected rank-and-file members, (3) shall invite the DSA National Harassment and Grievance Officer (HGO) to participate, (4) shall include chapter HGOs, (5) not include members who are in positions of leadership, either in their chapter or nationally, (6) be as diverse as possible, including members from varying ages, geographic regions, genders, race and ethnicities, sexual orientation, socio-economic statuses, members who are Individuals with Disabilities (IwDs); and Be it further resolved, two interim coordinators shall be elected by this convention, who shall be responsible for ensuring that the CRCWG is formed according to this resolution, and who shall serve for a term that lasts until the CRCWG is formed; and Be it further resolved, the CRCWG shall receive conflict resolution training and/or materials from multiple leftist, socialist, and/or anti-capitalist groups, as well as materials developed by locals, in order to prepare them to develop DSA’s program; and Be it further resolved, the development of the Conflict Resolution training program by the CRCWG shall: (1) incorporate at least 2 rounds of feedback, during which DSA membership shall have the opportunity to review the work of the CRCWG, provide feedback and make suggestions; and (2) include making monthly progress reports to members and the NPC via the DSA discussion forum; and

[PDF page 21] Background Information Additional Materials Be it further resolved, the resulting Conflict Resolution training program shall incorporate topics including: Conflict and reconciliation, Trauma and trauma- sensitivity, Privilege and anti oppression, De-escalation, and Codes of conduct and community agreements; and Be it finally resolved, the resulting training program shall be suitable for a variety of modalities, including in-person and online. Whereas, the structures of oppression (including capitalism, patriarchy, imperialism, and white supremacy) under which we live lead to maladaptive coping strategies and flawed ways of relating to one another; and Whereas, conflict cannot be avoided as members from diverse backgrounds and ideological perspectives organize together in a big-tent organization; and Whereas, socialist organizations and movements must be prepared to face agents provocateurs and intentional attempts by Capital to sow discord in movements that threaten it; and Whereas, conflict must be resolved: we must manage it, learn from it, and process it in a productive manner; Whereas, members have self-reported that they feel conflict resolution is inadequate locally and nationally; Whereas, the National Grievance Officer has received a larger number of grievances and complaints than originally expected; and Whereas, the structure created by Resolution 33 is limited in scope and application and doesn’t cover issues that don’t rise to the level of a grievance. Goals and Outcome Measures: ○ By October 1, 2019, the CRCWG shall be formed ○ By January 1, 2020, at least 1 round of member feedback shall have been completed ○ By April 1, 2020, a DSA Conflict Resolution Training curriculum will be developed and released to chapters, organizing committees, pre-OCs, and at-large members ○ By June 15, 2020, DSA Conflict Resolution trainings will be developed ○ By Convention 2021, 70% of chapters will have had at least one HGO or other member participate in a Conflict Resolution ‘Train the Trainers’ event ○ Conflict Resolution training shall be provided at national and regional DSA events, such as regional conferences, pre-convention conferences, the Activist Conference and Convention

[PDF page 22] ○ By Convention 2021, Conflict Resolution training will have been provided on at least 2 district calls for each region ○ By October 1, 2021, 70% of DSA chapters will have implemented Conflict Resolution programs, training, and education.

Staff Costs $10,761 Processing payments, trouble shooting, coordinating with and assisting new groups get set up, following through to ensure compliance and coordination between DSA and YDSA chapters. 12% Overhead $1,291 Direct Costs $37,500 Direct payments to chapters. Be it further resolved, DSA will provide $500 per year to each YDSA chapter affiliated with a DSA chapter and further: a) By default, funds shall be distributed to the DSA local that the YDSA chapter is affiliated with.

YDSA chapters based in schools shall indicate to the Youth Section Committee of start dates for school terms they plan to be active for during the next year in their application. Be it finally resolved, DSA may recuperate funds from a DSA chapter by withholding future distributions of any kind to the DSA local, up to $5000, if the local is found to be withholding or misappropriating funds that were disbursed for a YDSA chapter’s use. Whereas: • YDSA members represent the most in-debt generation in all human history and, as such, do not have much disposable cash to support their chapter. • YDSA chapters do not benefit from dues splitting structure like DSA chapters do. • Unlike DSA chapters, most YDSA chapters do not have a secure place to hold their money such as a bank account due to not being registered as an individual 501(c)4. Additionally, universities that do offer to hold money for YDSA chapters in their Bursar’s office do so to hold power over the YDSA chapter. • University YDSA groups are dependent on the political whims of their host university for funding and high school YDSA groups have no avenue to receive funding other than by accepting donations. • A significant amount of YDSA members have expressed a lack of support as a complaint against the national organization, including ROSE at George Mason, a former YDSA chapter that has dissociated partly due to this issue.

Resolution #25 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Childcare” by Laura C. of Chicago DSA; Bria D. of Boston DSA; Logan Y. of New Orleans DSA. Staff Costs $37,305 National campaign - 1/2 time staffer 12% Overhead $4,477 Direct Costs $20,000 Campaign materials. Total Cost $61,781 Authors’ Cost Estimate $20,000, staff time for coordinating campaign work in Resolved #1 and project work in coordination with SFWG in Resolved #2. Resolve Be it therefore resolved: 1. That DSA prioritize the fight for guaranteed paid parental leave and public universal child care and preschool, and dedicate resources, including staff time and $10,000 over the next two years, to develop a national campaign for federal, state, and local legislation guaranteeing paid parental leave and free, high-quality child care and preschool for all children; 2. That DSA require endorsed candidates to support guaranteed paid parental leave and public universal child care and preschool and encourage candidates and elected officials to develop universal (not means-tested) policies to that effect; 3. That DSA’s National Labor Commission or DSA members active in labor organizing and the Socialist Feminist Working Group or a sub-committee thereof collaborate to develop a feminist labor strategy to support efforts by domestic and child care workers to organize and improve their wages and working conditions; 4. That DSA dedicate national resources, including staff time and $10,000 to be spent at the direction of the Socialist Feminist Working Group in coordination with the NPC and national staff as well as members that have developed existing child watch programs, to: a. develop or modify and disseminate child watch materials for chapters, starting with the adaptation of existing chapter initiatives, b. train members to provide child watch services at chapter meetings and events, c. help chapters navigate statewide requirements for providing such services, and d. make child watch programs as inclusive as possible of disabled children and children with other needs; 5. That the Socialist Feminist Working Group or a sub-committee thereof will establish

[PDF page 49] Background Information a timeline and milestones for child watch program progress in coordination with the NPC and national staff, with the goal of working towards at least 75% of chapters having at least one member trained in child watch programming, and 50% of chapters having a regular child watch program, providing child watch for at least every chapter- wide meeting, by August 1, 2020. WHEREAS, 1. Our socialism is feminist, pro-worker, and dedicated to fighting against the burdens of capitalism for all parents and caregivers, particularly for women of the working class, who provide disparate amounts of reproductive labor, including child care; 2. The United States is one of the only countries in the world that does not require workplaces to offer paid parental leave to workers; 3. Low wages require most parents and caregivers to work full-time or more than full-time outside the home, causing them to rely on paid care for their children, or to rely upon the uncompensated labor of extended relatives or community members who may already be burdened by multiple obligations under capitalism; 4. Daycare and other forms of child care are expensive, costing more than in-state tuition at a four-year public college in 33 states, and are an undue burden on the working class; 5. Child care workers often receive low wages, are deeply exploited by difficult working conditions, are disproportionately women of color or immigrants, may not be eligible to unionize under the NLRA, often work in the informal sector, and often struggle to find affordable or adequate care for their own children while they care for the children of others; 6. Domestic and child care work is a key, largely unorganized sector of the economy, related to other female-dominated sectors of reproductive labor such as nursing and teaching; 7. The capitalist economy relies upon the unpaid or underpaid reproductive labor of people who can become pregnant and people who take on caregiving roles to reproduce its workforce; 8. Providing free, high-quality universal child care and preschool would reduce the reliance of working parents on their workplaces for wages and child care benefits, thus shoring up worker power; 9. Socialism recognizes that childrearing should be a communal undertaking, and that by providing welcoming and supportive spaces for children, we can support both those children’s own social, political, and emotional development, along with ameliorating their primary caregivers’ alienation and atomization under capitalism; 10. Our own organizing spaces must be inclusive, accessible, and welcoming to people of all ages, including families with children, and we must begin educating and valuing the input of the next generation of Democratic Socialists.

Resolution #32 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Labor Strategy and the DSLC” by Andrew P. of Columbus DSA; Marsha N. & Jonah F. of NYC DSA; Natalie M. of Philly DSA; Jane S. of Detroit DSA:, JP K. & Abby A. of Chicago DSA. Therefore be it resolved that the DSLC will focus on pursuing the rank and file strategy. The rank-and-file strategy argues that socialists’ central focus should be on identifying and developing a layer of rank and file leaders who can organize in the workplace on a day-to-day basis. This day-to-day organizing plays a crucial role in creating workers’ sense of being part of something bigger — not just a union, but a working class — that is capable of fighting, winning, and ultimately ruling. Therefore, the DSLC will continue to create general educational materials for DSA. Teaching people about the labor movement is a critical part of the DSLC’s mission. We need to educate members about the connection between the labor movement and the socialist movement. Our members need to understand how today’s labor movement functions, including its constraints as well as its possibilities. Therefore, the DSLC will create materials explaining the rank and file strategy and how members can participate. One existing example is the “Why Socialists Should Become Teachers” pamphlet. The DSLC will create materials arguing for socialists to take jobs in different union workplaces, a pamphlet on how to start a union in a non- union workplace, and report backs from members who do this work. Therefore the DSLC will create a Speakers Bureau to educate DSA members. The DSLC will find speakers who are knowledgeable and make it easy for chapters to connect with them. The goal will be to have speakers throughout the country so travel costs will be minimal. Chapters can apply to the DSLC to help with travel costs if they are hosting a traveling speaker. Therefore: The DSLC will create committees or discussion groups based on people’s jobs. This will allow members to share experiences and ideas, with the goal of joint action in the future. Therefore the national organization will help the DSLC with labor mapping. National will change its intake membership form to ask about people’s job and union connection.

[PDF page 63] Background Information National will also conduct a survey of current members. Therefore the DSLC will encourage chapters to support strikes and will produce a pamphlet about best practices for doing so. Strike support can build connections between workers and educate our members about unions. Therefore, the DSLC will make use of Labor Notes’ organizing training. These trainings will allow our members to make connections with other workers and develop the skills needed to organize. The DSLC will help chapter labor committees fundraise to send members to the April 2020 Labor Notes Conference and to participate in Labor Notes activities such as local Troublemakers Schools. Therefore, the DSLC will help chapters create Jobs Programs where members are mentored and supported. First, the DSLC will help chapters survey their area and determine the strategic sectors in their area where multiple members could get jobs. Second, the DSLC will train chapters on how to support members who are joining those sectors and provide training on how experienced workers can support new workers. Third, the DSLC will facilitate national communication and where possible coordination of members working in the same “industry” (e.g., K-12 schools). New York City DSA has begun such a jobs program that other chapters could consult as a possible model. Therefore DSA will increase the resources available for the DSLC. The DSLC shall have a permanent staff person to aid in its work within 4 months of the convention. The staffer will work on building labor branches and labor working groups, help build a national/regional communications structure, and provide guidance & resources to labor branches/working groups about projects they can undertake, including M4A, Bernie, promoting r&f jobs, and educational events. Additionally the DSLC and the NPC will create a plan within 6 months for how to sustainably hire more staff to do labor work. Whereas working people, the vast majority of society, have in their workplaces the structural power to attack capitalists’ profits and an interest in replacing capitalism with socialism. Organizing in and with the labor movement is therefore necessary to abolish capitalism. Whereas DSA created the Democratic Socialist Labor Commission to lead organizing work nationally within the labor movement. Since the last convention the DSLC has worked hard to improve our organizing capacity, but the DSLC’s limited resources have been a barrier and it needs more resources and political direction to better accomplish its work.

Support political candidates & organizations that aid in the fight for a radical GND and, in electoral campaigns in which DSA participates, agitate for elements of a radical GND described in the DSAEWG’s Guiding Principles. H. Direct the GNDCC, in partnership with the DSAEWG, DSA staff, & each region’s field organizer, to provide support to chapters with analyzing their local contexts, developing individual climate/environmental justice plans, & counseling on implementation tactics. Provide education & mentorship to help chapters develop organizing strategies, knowledge, & skills most relevant to implementing radical GND efforts in their localities, recognizing the varying political terrains they face. Help develop materials & resources for local ecosocialist campaigns that can cohere as part of the broader struggle for a GND. Facilitate collaboration & political interaction between chapters working on similar campaigns, & between chapters & allied groups outside DSA. I. Direct the GNDCC & designated staff to work with national working groups & appropriate DSA bodies to develop alliances of solidarity & cooperation that build an anti-imperialist, anti-racist, feminist, working class, internationalist movement here & abroad for an ecologically thriving & just world.

BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) endorse the cross-chapter campaign around the creation of the Great Lakes Authority, a regional-planning agency enacted through federal legislation under the umbrella of the “Green New Deal” with the mandate to bring green union jobs, environmental justice, and sustainable economic development to the Great Lakes region of the United States, consistent with DSA’s Guiding Principles of an Ecosocialist Green New Deal. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that DSA shall assist those chapters involved in this campaign with reasonable material resources, including funding and staff time, to further the campaign. WHEREAS the Great Lakes basin is home to precious natural resources, including the Great Lakes (which contain one-fifth of the world’s freshwater and provide potable water to over 40 million people), 55 million acres of productive land, and myriad low- carbon recreation options. WHEREAS the Great Lakes Region (Michigan and portions of Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin) overlaps substantially with the “Rust Belt,” which has been ravaged for decades by free trade deals, deindustrialization, and corporate pollution, and has yet to recover from the Great Recession of 2008. WHEREAS the Rust Belt’s long economic decline -- combined with the increasing regional impact of the climate crisis -- has produced a host of calamities, including the degradation of our air, water, and ecosystems; the privatization of both essential public services and natural resources; decrepit roads and bridges; inadequate mass transit; a housing crisis; the abandonment of entire communities. WHEREAS “market solutions” and “benevolent billionaires” have not and cannot address these problems, and have in fact exacerbated them, and only massive public

[PDF page 83] investment and government planning can restore the region’s economy, environment, and infrastructure. WHEREAS when General Motors announced plant closings and mass layoffs in 2018, Detroit DSA organized a demonstration demanding that the government seize the Detroit plant by eminent domain and use it to address the climate emergency and build green infrastructure, and a coalition of environmental, labor, and community organizations in Detroit formed around these demands and this radical vision for a Green New Deal. WHEREAS Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-13), a member of DSA who was part of that coalition, asked Detroit DSA to develop legislative ideas in furtherance of a Green New Deal and to present them to her and her staff. WHEREAS Detroit DSA determined that the Rust Belt should be the “Engine of the Green New Deal,” meaning that much of the green infrastructure (solar panels, wind turbines, electric transit, etc.) needed to avert a climate catastrophe should be manufactured in the Rust Belt, where millions of people already have manufacturing expertise and experience, and hundreds of underused or idled manufacturing facilities already exist. WHEREAS Detroit DSA determined that this goal should be achieved through what it calls the “Great Lakes Authority” (GLA), a new, federal, regional planning agency (enacted through federal legislation under the umbrella of the “Green New Deal”) with the mandate to bring green union jobs, environmental justice, and sustainable economic development to the Great Lakes region. WHEREAS the GLA would prioritize (1) creating green, prevailing-wage, union-backed jobs, including in green manufacturing, (2) creating millions of zero-carbon public housing units and weatherizing existing homes, and (3) restoring the region’s infrastructure, including its energy and water systems; its roads, bridges, and waterways; and its public transit, and be guided by the principles of (1) local control, (2) worker dignity, and (3) a just transition. WHEREAS Detroit DSA has shared the idea of the GLA with great success in print and social media, as well as in person at labor events, in community forums and town halls, at the Midwest DSA Regional Convention, etc. WHEREAS, in light of these efforts, DSA members from across the Rust Belt (including Detroit, Chicago, Milwaukee, Toledo, Flint, Cleveland, Columbus, Huron Valley, Cincinnati, and Pittsburgh) are now actively thinking through the idea of the GLA, what such a unifying demand could mean for our ecosocialist work, and organizing to make the GLA a reality.

Do you commit to working for these principles at the national (and where appropriate, state) level? 3. [For local candidates:] Do you support repealing relevant similar local laws where they exist (such as “right to work” legislation)? 4. Do you support legislation for the provision of universal, tuition-free child care? 5. Do you support the College for All Act, and specifically making public universities, colleges, and trade schools tuition-free and reducing student debt? [For local candidates:] Do you commit to fully funding public schools, and halting

Resolution #58 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Progressive Dues Sharing” by Charles D. & Elizabeth M. of San Francisco DSA. Staff Costs $3,587 Resolution misunderstands present dues sharing practice, which is not based on a flat rate per member but rather the actual total monthly dues collected from members within the jurisdiction of each chapter. Staff time would be required to develop a mechanism to operationalize the goals of the resolution. 12% Overhead $430 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $4,017 Author’s Cost Estimate Resolve This does not affect the total amount of dues disbursed back to chapters. Rather, it changes the amount received by each chapter, so that smaller chapters receive more and larger chapters receive less, with the sum of these changes netting out to zero. In that sense, it would not alter the organization’s budget in any way, although it would obviously likely change individual chapters’ budgets. We resolve, the current dues sharing system, passed in Resolution 21 at the 2017 National Convention, shall be amended such that chapters shall no longer receive a fixed disbursement per member. Rather, the amount each chapter shall receive per member from the total funds allocated for dues sharing (currently 20% of monthly national dues) shall be determined by chapter size, with smaller chapters receiving more money per member than larger chapters. Each time dues kickbacks are disbursed to chapters (at present quarterly), the spreadsheet used to calculate dues disbursements shall be updated with the most up-to-date chapter sizes, and dues disbursements shall be calculated using this spreadsheet or another that implements the same calculation. An explainer of the mechanism behind the spreadsheet is also available. We further resolve, the “progressiveness” level by chapter size as delineated in the spreadsheet shall begin with the values with which it is currently populated. Beginning with the passage of this amendment, the Budgetary committee shall have the option of meeting before every quarterly disbursement to adjust the progressiveness levels. If the committee chooses to adjust these numbers, they must provide a written statement to the membership of the organization justifying the changes they are making. We further resolve, the progressiveness levels shall not be set such that the ratio of the dues per member (ie total dues disbursed to chapter divided by total chapter size) received by the smallest chapter to the dues per member received by the largest chapter are lower than 3 or higher than 6, provided that the ratio of the size of the largest chapter to the size of the smallest chapter does not fall lower than 10. If the chapter size

[PDF page 114] Background Information distribution ever changes such that this becomes the case, the budgetary committee must change the progressiveness such that this is no longer the case. This is just to ensure that the dues sharing scheme never impacts large chapters in a way that would cut their dues too drastically, while also ensuring that the progressive spirit of this proposal cannot be watered down too drastically by the budgetary committee. We finally resolve, this amendment shall be annulled if the membership of the largest chapter in the organization falls below 500 members. Smaller chapters presently frequently do not have enough money, even in total between their kickback from national and donations solicited from members, to afford things like childcare or even the rental fee for a space in which to hold meetings. There is often a lower bound to the cost of these necessities of a functioning chapter, even if the chapter’s membership is in the single digits, and the current flat dues-sharing scheme is insufficient to address this. Something like the “Pass the Hat” proposal being considered serves to assuage this to a degree, and this proposal compliments that one should it pass, but progressive dues sharing serves to address this issue whether or not chapters receive a fixed stipend, and is also designed to scale as the organization continues to grow. The first 10 members of a chapter receiving significantly more per member than the last 10 members of a 1,000 person chapter would serve to make the operation of a 10-member chapter, which is a necessity in order to build a socialist movement everywhere in the country, significantly easier. There are significant economies of scale enjoyed by larger chapters to which smaller chapters do not have access. Childcare and space-rental are two examples of several components of the ability to have an effective local, and they also have significant economies of scale. The total cost of things like childcare, space rental, printing, and refreshments for a 500 member meeting is typically significantly less than five times that of a 100 person meeting, so disbursing five times as much funds to the larger chapter in this example would be, in this sense, regressive. It is imperative that we materially support comrades who are organizing in areas that are rural, especially hostile to left-wing ideas, or both. Larger chapters, which often just have to literally “pass the hat” to raise enough to cover their costs, should be the ones to step in and provide this support, at least in part. There are a number of other resolutions being proposed that aim towards this same goal; as a purely redistributive measure of an existing funding source, this resolution is designed to be compatible with all of them. There’s no mass movement in the cities alone; we in large chapters must support our comrades in small chapters, not just with our words but with our pocketbooks as well.

Resolution #64 Title & Author “Housing For All: Analysis and Recommendations for DSA Chapters” by Sara R. of Chicago DSA; Karen N., Celia W., & Jennifer L. of NYC DSA; Richard M. of East Bay DSA; Alicia H. of St. Louis DSA; Beth H. of Boston DSA. Budget Analysis Staff Costs $0 No additional up front costs. 12% Overhead $0 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $0 Resolve BE IT RESOLVED THAT: We must fight to dismantle the private property market and fight for housing as a human right. This means that everyone has an affordable place to live; it means resident self-determination and control — through strong tenant unions, rent controls, democratically controlled social housing, and alternative community ownership models. We believe that the struggle for fully decommodified housing requires a struggle for renters’ rights in the short and medium term. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT: DSA chapters should fight for rent control laws that limit rent increases, include enforcement mechanisms and protect against eviction. Rent control allows tenants the opportunity to remain in their communities even as they become susceptible to gentrification. We demand rent control because it is uniquely able to unite a mass working-class movement, and to ease the path to social housing. By challenging the profits of landlords and their direct power over our rents, we can also challenge the political power of the real estate industry. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT: We believe that only universal social housing can provide affordable homes to the entire working class. Federal, state and local governments should spend public funds directly on creating millions of publicly- and socially-owned housing developments that are permanently affordable, democratically controlled, and available to residents of all incomes. Since the 1970s, the US government has privatized public housing and subsidized private landlords. However, we can draw on models from around the world to create an alternative system of social housing in the US, both by bringing existing market housing under social control and by building new social housing. BE IT FINALLY RESOLVED THAT: When possible chapters should pursue these strategies for housing organizing, taking into account that each chapter faces a unique political landscape and housing market. • Incorporate the housing crisis into their political analysis and candidate selection process, and encourage DSA-endorsed candidates to include rent control and social housing in their platform.

[PDF page 124] Background Information • Join or help launch campaigns for tenant protections through universal rent control, just cause eviction, and enforcement of health and safety regulations. • Target bad landlords and lead campaigns that call attention to their abusive practices. • Highlight the influence of real estate money in politics, either by calling on candidates and elected officials to pledge to reject real estate donations, or by targeting politicians who refuse to do so. • Organize for a Green New Deal that will repair public housing and create new social housing. • Promote equitable and democratic development, including maximum affordability, abolishing tax incentives for for-profit developers, and community control of land. • Support tenant organizing efforts; strengthen DSA’s connection to the existing tenant movement while helping it to expand and radicalize. • Work to address long-lasting racial discrimination in housing and support full funding and enforcement of fair housing and civil rights laws. WHEREAS: The ongoing commodification of land and housing is driving a housing crisis that harms millions of working people across the country and reproduces racial inequities. The neoliberal response—rolling back local regulations and starving public housing authorities while letting Wall Street buy up private housing—only boosts the profits of the real estate investor class. As a result, homelessness is widespread, rents are skyrocketing, and entire communities are being displaced. In the wake of the foreclosure crisis, private equity firms and other corporate investors have played an increasingly large role in the housing market, making rental housing an asset for global capital. AND WHEREAS: Rental housing is a key site of struggle for many working-class people. Housing issues affect DSA members and the working class directly, and organizing around them gives us the opportunity to confront real estate capital and build coalitions with other tenants. Running electoral campaigns that highlight housing for all as a demand and reject real estate donations helps DSA connect with a broader base of tenants and link housing to other issues as part of a socialist platform. We hope to help make tenants as a political force that can challenge the power of the real estate industry in politics.

Resolution #69 Title & Author Budget Analysis “YDSA Staff Expansion” by Ajmal A. of Metro DC DSA and Elliot G. of Chattanooga DSA. Staff Costs $301,308 Time spent recruiting, interviewing, and operational onboarding new staff + direct costs of 4 staff. 12% Overhead $36,157 Direct Costs Total Cost $337,465 Resolve Therefore be it resolved, YDSA’s NCC and authors of this resolution will create a proposed plan as a part of a joint DSA/YDSA personnel committee to staff YDSA on a one year timeline and negotiate wages for each staffing position and create the positions for hire. Due to YDSA’s conventions occurring yearly, staffing must be done within this period. The staffing needs that the DSA/YDSA personnel committee will be tasked with filling are as follows from above: Lead Organizer, Administrator, Political Organizer, and Field Organizer Background Information Whereas, YDSA hasn’t had a staffer for the past year, as YDSA’s former staffer was transitioned to the position of DSA regional staffer. Only recently has a hiring process been established for a new YDSA staffer. YDSA is a full organization with a constitution, membership rolls, and political priorities. YDSA has grown, and will continue to grow, as more young people begin to identify with socialism. Our current staff situation is untenable. YDSA requires its own staff independent of DSA staff in order for its administrative and organizational work to function effectively. This will ameliorate administrative bottlenecks, enable further nationally coordinated political action, and bolster local YDSA organizing efforts. YDSA’s staffing requires the following positions: 1) Lead Organizer: The Lead Organizer would oversee the administration of YDSA alongside the YDSA National co-chairs, and ensure that the NCC has the support it needs to process chapter applications, organize the winter conference and other YDSA national (and potentially regional) events, communicating with staff and committees, and other various tasks. The YDSA Lead Organizer would not be directly supervised

[PDF page 135] by DSA’s national director, but would be collectively accountable to the rest of DSA staff — similar to the DSA national director. YDSA staff positions would also fall under the purview of YDSA’s Lead Organizer, and the YDSA Lead Organizer would provide support to all other YDSA staffers to ensure that they’re able to carry their work out effectively as well. 2) Administrator: The YDSA administrator will keep comprehensive and updated lists of membership, chapters, and membership information. Membership informations includes: major, graduation date, career choice, and graduation plans. Additionally, the admin would be in charge of outreach to YDSA members, so as to ensure that all YDSA members receive updates from the NCC and National Subcommittees. When necessary, the administrator would also help YDSA members transition onto DSA organizing post- graduation. For example, YDSA members interested in pursuing the rank-and-file strategy post-graduation would be assisted by the YDSA Administrator in getting in touch with the YDSA labor subcommittee, and potentially the DSLC. 3) Political organizer: The Political Organizer would be responsible for assisting YDSA political committees/subcommittees and coordinating between them. The Political Organizer would help ensure that all political work is within a timeline, facilitate resources, coordinate work and communication between committees to avoid redundancies and to ensure that campaigns complement one another. The Political Organizer would also coordinate between YDSA campaign committees/subcommittees (College for All, Bernie, etc), each ROC region, and the chapters within regions to help formulate chapter- or region-specific plans for actions. They would also help chapters determine how to run campaigns, whether they are national priorities or not (adjunct/dining worker unionization campaign, fossil fuel divestment campaign, etc), as well as create trainings for chapters to emulate. 4) Field Organizer: YDSA chapters desperately need a face to national, and having a field organizer would significantly address this. The Field Organizer would visit chapters to assist them in their campaigns, report local conditions to the NCC, and connect local chapters with other organizations, such as labor unions. The Field Organizer would work extensively with the Political Organizer, essentially doing their work on the ground. A Field Organizer would be indispensable when it comes to expanding YDSA, whether it be by visiting HBCU campuses or Community Colleges, where they can identify potential organizers and assist in the creation of chapters. Without staff, initiatives like these would fail to materialize. Our Field Organizer is perhaps one of the most crucial positions amongst staffing to help YDSA carry out our work and priorities we vote on at the YDSA convention.

Resolution #70 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Mass Strike for Reproductive Justice” by Staff Costs $861 Only cost called for is time to coordinate comms and the national website, so estimate a few hours per month, same as existing support to national working groups (internal and external communications, website updates, Zoom calls, organizing coaching.) 12% Overhead $103 Direct Costs Total Cost $964 Resolve BE IT RESOLVED THAT: DSA endorses the call for a mass strike for reproductive rights and will begin organizing in anticipation of a challenge to Roe vs. Wade at the Supreme Court by taking the following actions: CAMPAIGN STRUCTURE The NPC will recognize the Mass Strike for Reproductive Rights Committee comprised of members of DSA chapters in states affected by abortion bans, the nation-wide Socialist Feminist Working Group, and labor activists in DSA. This committee will be comprised of labor, research, coalition, and media subcommittees and an organizing subcommittee comprised of two point people from each of these groups. STRATEGY We believe we will have 2-3 years to prepare for a challenge to Roe vs. Wade at the Supreme Court. DSA must use this time to build the campaign infrastructure and relationships to coalition partners needed to create a mass movement for reproductive rights that is capable of creating mass unrest and financial damages. While more work is needed to bring in the key stakeholders in order to fully flush out our campaign strategy, the basic strategy will have three prongs and will escalate over a series of actions as the abortion bans work their way through the court system. Rank and File Strategy Working with the DSLC and other labor activists, we will identify rank and file members who are interested in agitating around the idea for a mass strike. One strategy for developing rank and file leadership is through consciousness raising groups. Workers could organize CR groups to discuss how issues in their workplace relate to issues of social reproduction. From these groups, organizers

[PDF page 137] Background Information can build leadership committees to agitate for a strike around workplace demands that help workers draw connections between work and social reproduction. These demands could include: parental leave, sexual harassment, equal pay, healthcare, and scheduling control. More research needs to be done on the financial holdings of the politicians, judges, and outside groups who are propagating anti-abortion legislation, but we know these people are wealthy capitalists. By researching their holdings, we can target our labor outreach in order to do the most financial damage with the least amount of people. Reproductive Rights and Coalition Work DSA had 75 teams raised a total of $137,472 for NNAF this spring. This represents a nascent network that could be developed further to coordinate direct actions and mutual aid networks. DSA chapters also have connections to local abortion funds, reproductive rights organizations, and other coalition partners who are either already engaging in direct action or could be interested in joining in our actions. Using DSA's fundraising and mobilizing capacities we can build trust with outside organizations. Through relationship building, we can help tie local work to our movement for a mass strike and push existing work in a more militant direction, one that uses direct action to impede the functions of society. Media Strategy Since the 2016 election there have been several media moments where the atrocities of the Trump administration captured the attention of the masses and the resulting outcry was able to keep the worst actions from moving forward, at least temporarily. We know that over the next few years as the abortion bans work their way through the courts there will be natural moments of escalation. Our job is to keep media attention on the abortion bans and keep the public from slowly going numb as they are overwhelmed by continual onslaught of rightwing extremism. We do this with grand calls to actions. Our media team will recruit spokespeople with a national presence and connections to DSA, such as Sara Nelson and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez*, to call on unions to strike. We can also solicit DSA-connected feminist scholars like Tithi Bhattacharya (Feminism of the 99%) and Jenny Brown (Birth Strike)** to submit articles to sympathetic publications to make the case why social reproduction is a labor issue and call for a mass strike. WHEREAS: The Right in the US is waging war against reproductive rights. At the time of our writing, abortion bans have been implemented in Ohio, Georgia, Alabama, Louisiana, and Missouri. These bans are the result of decades of attacks — increasing restrictive TRAP laws, firebombs at abortion clinics, the assassination of providers, the prosecution of miscarriage, and the setting of a legal framework to bestow “personhood” on fetuses. The intention of these orchestrated attacks is explicit: the repeal of Roe v. Wade. It is highly likely these bans will go to the intensely undemocratic Supreme Court in which anti-choice Conservatives have majority. As socialists, we must see these attacks as what they are: an act of class war targeting the most vulnerable.

[PDF page 138] Abortion bans do not protect the sanctity of life — they conscript people to give birth against their will and criminalize normal behaviors while pregnant. Not only have we seen the degradation of our reproductive rights, but we have also seen the erosion of our access to affordable housing, child care, good public schools, and a clean and safe environment. Reproductive labor is largely an unpaid and unrecognized contribution to society and abortion is our right to strike from unfair working conditions. We affirm the right of all people to control the conditions of their reproduction, including the rights of those who have children to deliver them safely into the world, and care for them as they grow. We affirm the bodily autonomy of migrants, not only to have abortion care, safely deliver their babies, and remain with their children, but to move freely to seek a better life. We affirm the right of all people across the globe to live without threat of U.S. imperialism. Abortion bans do not protect the sanctity of life— only socialist feminism does. *Sara Nelson and AOC have not yet been contacted about this proposal ** Tithi Bhattacharya and Jenny Brown have discussed this proposal with the authors and are supportive of the idea of a mass strike, but have not yet directly committed to the project

Resolution #82 Title & Author Budget Analysis “DSA National Electoral Priority Resolution” by Michael K. & Abdullah Y. of NYC DSA; Tim Z. of Honolulu DSA; Hannah A. of Lawrence KS. DSA Staff Costs $37,305 Appears to require priority campaign level support as exists now - 1/2 staffer. 12% Overhead $4,477 Direct Costs $0 Total Cost $41,781 Resolve Background Information Therefore, be it resolved that: 1) The NPC should expand the work of the National Electoral Committee in supporting chapters’ efforts to develop and run viable openly socialist candidates for office, on Democratic, independent, or other ballot lines. The priority of the NEC should be to support locals in building electoral infrastructure that is democratically accountable to the membership and engages as many people as possible. 2) DSA cannot engage in mass politics without building solidarity with aligned political forces and the broader working class. Wherever possible, DSA chapters should work to build diverse, multiracial electoral coalitions grounded in working-class institutions, unions and community groups. In selecting candidates to support, DSA chapters should be encouraged to prioritize races that have the potential to form a broader multiracial coalition 3) DSA chapters must be given wide discretion to support candidates whose campaigns offer strategic opportunities within their concrete local contexts, but chapters are encouraged to prioritize candidates who stand for class-struggle politics and strive to support open socialists wherever possible. 4) DSA should recognize that electoral work is not a strategy or an end in itself, but a tactic to advance broader movement struggles, and should link electoral work to our core strategic goals, like abolishing ICE, implementing the Green New Deal and passing Medicare for All. 5) DSA should continue to pursue electoral organizing as one of its national priorities for the next two years, in order to advance a political revolution up and down the ballot and in every region of the country. Two years ago at its previous national convention, DSA chose electoral work as one of its three national priorities. Since that time, DSA chapters across the country have achieved extraordinary successes in municipal, state and federal elections. DSA has not only helped elect committed leftists all over the US, but has built movement power, sharpened organizing skills and expanded its membership in doing so. DSA must continue to reject the false opposition between movement work and elections. State power and movement power condition each other; grassroots movements can alter the context in which elected officials operate, and legislative power affects the possibilities for democratic social change. Furthermore, electoral work can build the

[PDF page 157] power and visibility of the socialist movement. Many people who are open to radical politics first enter organized politics through election work, and DSA’s size and strength today is a testament to how left-wing campaigns like those of Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez can inspire people to get involved in organized left politics for the first time. In a nation where politics is increasingly dominated by the billionaire class, DSA’s electoral effectiveness is tied to the volunteer power of our chapters. Ensuring that left- wing elected officials will remain accountable to the working class requires building a strong organizational infrastructure and robust coalitions determined not only to elect working-class candidates but also to advance an ambitious political program between elections.

Resolution #86 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Prioritize National Working Groups” by Johannes M. (Silicon Valley); Michelle B. (Orlando), Ravi A. (Long Beach) Staff Costs $74,610 Time to manage potentially rapidly increasing numbers of national working groups would require a new full time staffer. 12% Overhead $8,953 Direct Costs - Total Cost $83,563 Author’s Cost Estimate This resolution would require NPC time to hear working group petitions and budget requests. Separate tracking will mean ongoing labor by the Secretary-Treasurer and oversight by the NPC. Providing forums for Working Groups should require minimal labor, as we already have suitable forums at discussion.dsausa.org. If a Working Group requests that its forum section be private, the Database Administrator and Tech Committee would need to work together to ensure access. It should be possible to create simple websites for Working Groups with about 8 hours of volunteer work each, given that suitable hosting and themes are already available to DSA. Conference call service subscriptions should total less than $2000, but if existing accounts can be used, this would incur no additional cost. Electronic voting would require a subscription or setting up a DSA-internal instance based on open-source code. (Loomio offers both options.) Other needs would be assessed separately by the Working Groups, National Tech Committee and other teams, and by the NPC. This is unpredictable and will emerge organically from the work. Inviting all members to discussion.dsausa.org entails at least one physical mailer or phone call to members who have unsubscribed from email. However, there is no further cost to including this link in ongoing email and letters, other than updating templates. Resolve Therefore be it resolved: As a priority, National DSA shall: (i) support national Working Groups and (ii) help foster new Working Groups for issues that members are already organizing for in their chapters. What is a Working Group?

[PDF page 164] Our power comes from local chapters, but our work has no borders. Working Groups shall connect members across chapters, and shall help facilitate and coordinate common work in relation to the Working Group’s mission. Working Groups shall not direct the work of chapters. In the context of National DSA, the term “Working Group” shall be a synonym for “Commission” as defined in the DSA Constitution. The only other kind of body that the NPC may create is a “committee”, governed by Robert’s Rules of Order. What kinds of support can Working Groups expect? National DSA shall provide internal communication tools for each Working Group, including electronic discussion forums and tools for debate and electronic voting. National DSA shall provide each Working Group with a simple website, access to conference call accounts, and other tech, based on Working Group needs and the capacity of the National Tech Committee. Working Groups shall be able to propose a budget to the NPC, and shall be able to raise funds to be managed separately by National DSA. How can I create a Working Group? Per the Bylaws, the NPC shall hear Working Group petitions if submitted by at least 10 members. The NPC shall publish guidelines help members craft successful petitions, and shall respond to petitions promptly. By October 1, 2019, the National Director shall encourage all members to use our official forums at discussion.dsausa.org to connect with each other to form Working Groups. A link to the forums shall be included prominently in all mass communications to members. The NPC may create temporary Working Group Exploratory Committees for issues that members are already organizing around locally. The mission of such Committees shall be to connect members to work towards chartering a Working Group, not to directly organize for the issue. What about existing groups and other priorities? Existing national groups working on an issue or campaign shall be considered Working Groups. This includes the Medicare for All Campaign, the Labor Commission, the National Electoral Committee, Democratic Socialists for Bernie, and the International Committee; and current issue-based Working Groups like the Ecosocialist Working Group. These Working Groups shall: • Be open to all members of DSA, except where the NPC or the authorizing motion restricts membership based on an affinity, as in the Veterans Working Group. • Be structured democratically. Their Steering Committees or similar bodies shall be elected by a proportional method, modified for applicable representation requirements; and the membership shall be able to initiate and participate in electronic votes. Working Groups shall keep minutes of their meetings and decisions, available to all members of DSA. Where other resolutions of the 2019 Convention create a “Working Group” or a similar body that executes a “Priority”, they shall be considered Working Groups in the sense of this resolution, and the above requirements for openness and democracy shall extend to these groups.

[PDF page 165] Background Information Let’s get to work! Local chapters are the heart of DSA, but to win we also need to be organized around issues that are national or international. The model that has worked best in DSA is that of a national Working Group that any member can join. The bottom-up process that led to the Guiding Principles for an Ecosocialist Green New Deal is a shining example of how this can work. Let’s live up to the needs of our members who want to organize together, and direct National DSA to make fostering and supporting our national Working Groups a priority.

Resolution #88 Title & Author Budget Analysis “Political Platform” by DSA NPC Staff Costs $18,652 Coordinating organization wide engagement in process - 1/4 staff time. 12% Overhead $2,238 Direct Costs - Total Cost $20,891 Resolve Background Information Therefore be it resolved The NPC shall oversee a process for drafting a concise political platform for DSA to adopt at our 2021 DSA Convention. The political platform shall include analysis, strategy, and a set of concrete demands that can guide the work of DSA chapters and DSA elected officials, cohere DSA’s practical activity and political identity, and serve as a basis for internal political education and external propaganda. The two-year platform drafting process shall involve wide participation from chapters and individual members in written debates, discussions on national zoom calls, and in- person meetings. Whereas In 2017, the NPC organized a process to draft the Priorities Resolution that involved some feedback from members — a straw poll and a zoom call were the main features — before submitting a document to the 2017 Convention. This took place over a few months leading up to the convention. However, different conditions in 2019 make this approach insufficient. The organization is much larger and more politically diverse than in 2017. Now a similarly short process would be more difficult and less effective in getting input and support from members. DSA should spend a longer time developing a programmatic document for the coming years. For reference DSA’s Resistance Rising strategy document, published in 2016, took years to develop collectively. Whereas Priorities resolutions served the organization well in the past by identifying three priority work areas. But now that DSA has entered political prominence with nearly 60,000 members and dozens of elected officials in office, we need a document that is broader and more substantive than the priorities resolution. Whereas It is essential that DSA continues to develop programmatic documents. A political platform containing analysis, strategy, and a set of concrete demands can serve several functions that are important for DSA going forward. First, it helps to cohere DSA’s many

[PDF page 168] chapters on the basis of a common political identity without mandating them all to carry out the same activities. Second, by clarifying our political identity publicly, we can attract new members, supporters, and allies who support some or all of our demands and are won over to a democratic socialist vision and strategy. Third, a platform would allow DSA to comprehensively shape the agendas of DSA candidates and elected officials, rather than inspiring just one or two of their demands. This would broaden the scope of socialist candidates’ political agenda while enhancing the level of accountability between DSA-endorsed candidates and DSA.
